Baby & Child

When a child gets sick after a shared meal

Updated: November 16, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

The morning after a family lunch, your toddler vomits. A cousin who was there has diarrhoea. Before trying to work out what was in the sandwiches, check how your child looks, how much they can drink and when they last passed urine. The meal may be a clue. The first decision is whether the child needs medical help now.

Check the child’s condition first

Get emergency help if the child is difficult to wake, has trouble breathing or develops sudden trouble swallowing, double vision or marked weakness after a possible food exposure. Green vomit, blood in vomit or severe, persistent abdominal pain also need emergency assessment. Tell the team about the meal, but leave the search for its source until help is arranged.

Get urgent medical advice for bloody diarrhoea, repeated vomiting that prevents drinking, or signs of dehydration such as much less urine than usual, a dry mouth, sunken eyes or unusual drowsiness. A baby younger than three months with a temperature of 38°C or higher needs urgent medical assessment. Infants, especially those under six months, can become dehydrated more quickly. Contact a clinician early if a baby is feeding poorly or you are worried.

Why the last thing they ate may not be the cause

Foodborne illness can cause nausea, vomiting, watery or bloody diarrhoea, cramping or fever. An infection spread directly from another person can cause much the same symptoms. Ask when symptoms started and who else is sick. Someone who shared only part of the meal, or who stayed home but was already ill, can be an important clue.

The time between eating and symptoms varies. For example, illness from a toxin produced by Staphylococcus bacteria can start within hours. Campylobacter infection often takes two to five days. Timing alone cannot identify the food or germ. Think back over meals, snacks, drinks and outings during the week before symptoms began.

Help a one- or two-year-old keep fluids down

If the child is awake and able to drink, offer small, frequent sips. A commercial oral rehydration solution replaces water and salts lost through vomiting or diarrhoea. If it comes as a powder, mix it with precisely the amount of safe water on the packet. Continue breastfeeding. A clinician or pharmacist can advise on the amount and product for your child.

Once rehydrated, a child can return to their usual foods and full-strength milk feeds as tolerated. Juice and fizzy drinks can make diarrhoea worse. Do not give an anti-diarrhoeal medicine to a young child or use leftover antibiotics. Bloody stools need assessment, and the choice of treatment depends on the cause. If even small sips will not stay down, seek medical help.

Record the details while they are easy to remember

Write down what the child ate and drank at home, at childcare and away from home, when symptoms began, and whether others became ill. Keep receipts or photographs of product labels, batch numbers and dates if available. Stop serving a suspected item. Ask the local public health or food safety service how to handle any leftovers they may want to test.

In an investigation of illness in 1996, researchers identified 70 cases of E. coli infection associated with unpasteurised commercial apple juice across several US states and one Canadian province. Comparing people’s exposures helped investigators identify the source. This was one outbreak. A child’s symptoms after drinking juice cannot by themselves establish what caused them. If several people became sick after the same event, contact the local service even if you do not know which food to name.

Watch for changes during recovery

The course depends on the cause and the child. With a typical stomach infection, vomiting often settles within a day or two, while diarrhoea may last several days. Look at whether the child is more alert, is drinking and is passing urine closer to their usual pattern. Seek advice sooner for deterioration, blood in the stool, returning symptoms or poor intake. You can call before a particular number of days has passed.

Use soap and water after changing nappies or helping with the toilet and before preparing food. Keep the child away from childcare or school while vomiting or diarrhoea continues, then follow local return guidance. Some identified infections require specific clearance. Ask the team what applies if the child’s illness is part of an outbreak.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Prioritise clinical signs of dehydration and other urgent symptoms.

Continue safe fluid replacement and follow the instructions for mixing oral rehydration solution.

Gather food histories and packaging information to help investigate suspected shared exposure.

How BeMama can help

BeMama follows a family lunch to show what helps a sick child immediately and what can help public health staff connect cases later.

When to seek help

Difficulty waking, trouble breathing or swallowing, double vision, marked weakness, green or bloody vomit or severe persistent abdominal pain need emergency assessment. Arrange urgent medical review for bloody diarrhoea, inability to drink or dehydration.

Evidence notes updated: November 16, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Check alertness, breathing, drinking and urine output before trying to identify the food.
  • Symptoms can begin well after the last meal. Note earlier foods, dates and who else is ill.
  • Use oral rehydration solution as directed and continue breastfeeding.
  • Report a suspected cluster to the local public health or food safety service.

Frequently asked questions

Which symptoms suggest food poisoning in a child?

Vomiting, diarrhoea, cramps or fever after a possible exposure can fit foodborne illness. Similar symptoms can spread between people. The timing, foods eaten, other cases and sometimes a stool test can help a clinician or public health team investigate.

When should I call a clinician for a toddler?

Seek urgent advice if your child has bloody diarrhoea, cannot keep down fluids, urinates much less than usual, is very sleepy or seems to be getting worse. Tell the clinician about recent meals, any other people who are sick, and the last wet nappy or toilet visit.

Which signs need emergency help?

Breathing difficulty, difficulty waking the child, sudden trouble swallowing, double vision or marked weakness need emergency help. Green vomit, bloody vomit or severe persistent abdominal pain also need emergency assessment. These signs can have causes other than food poisoning.

How many days will my child be ill?

There is no fixed duration. With ordinary gastroenteritis, vomiting often eases before diarrhoea, which can continue for several days. Ask for help at any point if your child cannot drink, seems dehydrated or develops a warning sign. Follow any instructions for the particular infection.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
